source_basis: Bullock, Martinez del Rio & Ayala 1989 Oecologia; DOI 10.1007/BF00379114
notes: Primary abstract distinguishes effective pollinators from pollen thieves and reports their changing abundance through the day.
Trigona spinipes is explicitly classified as a pollen and nectar thief and frequently excludes hummingbird pollinators.

source_basis: Eguiarte, Martinez del Rio & Arita 1987 Biotropica 19:74-82
notes: Primary study groups bees among floral parasites and reports an important negative effect through reduced pollination by secondary bird pollinators.

source_basis: Amela Garcia & Hoc 1998 Revista de Biologia Tropical 46:191-201
notes: Augochlorella collects pollen without touching stigmas and is explicitly classified as a pollen thief.

source_basis: Goldblatt et al. 2004 Plant Systematics and Evolution; DOI 10.1007/s00606-003-0067-1
notes: Fungus gnats are the primary pollinators; hoverflies and bumblebees usually behave as pollen robbers visiting only male-phase flowers.

source_basis: Lundgren, Razzak & Wiedenmann 2004 Environmental Entomology; DOI 10.1603/0046-225X-33.4.958
notes: Field study quantifies consumption of corn pollen by coccinellid predators during anthesis. No plant-fitness effect is claimed at this stage.
Staphylinid beetles remove substantial amounts of pollen but deposit none onto stigmas.
Primary study identifies Bombus haemorrhoidalis as effective and only pollinator while Apis cerana acts as a pollen robber.

source_basis: Torezan-Silingardi & Del-Claro 1998 Ciencia e Cultura 50:281-284; later direct source summaries
notes: The registered 1998 study is repeatedly reported as showing intense Apis pollen collection without stigma transfer, avoidance by native pollinators, and threatened fructification.
